document_title: Texas Tech says its AI aircraft maintenance tools have been provided to the Army
_note: Caption carried verbatim from caption.txt. Slide strings polished by the copywriter from storyboard.md and held to the claim quotes in claims.json. Every numeral is in claims.json or figures.json. Drawn to illustrate or drawn to no maker's design appears only on S1 and S2. Every result reads in testing. The tools are provided to the Army and never fielded or used.
caption:
37 percent reads like a failing grade.

Texas Tech worked with AVX Defense Technologies of Fort Worth on the Army's FleetSpace program. Together they developed an AI enabled planning tool for Army aviation. Texas Tech says a second tool tracks the remaining useful life of aircraft engines on its own. It recommends maintenance tied to the aviation technical manual. Texas Tech says both have been provided to the Army.

The 37 percent was never a grade. It is the share of missing and corrupted flight data the team's neural networks restored in testing. In testing they also predicted unplanned and 480 hour phase maintenance actions and cut data files by up to 73 percent.

Texas Tech's release names no result from service. If the Army runs them outside testing, how much of the result will be public?

#TexasTech #FortWorth #FleetSpace

S1.headline: AI maintenance tools, provided to the Army
S1.body: Texas Tech built two maintenance tools for Army aviation, one of them with AVX Defense Technologies of Fort Worth. Texas Tech says both have been provided to the Army. Engine drawn to no maker's design.
strings: AI maintenance tools, provided to the Army

Texas Tech built two maintenance tools for Army aviation, one of them with AVX Defense Technologies of Fort Worth. Texas Tech says both have been provided to the Army. Engine drawn to no maker's design.

S2.headline: Flight records arrive with holes
S2.body: Some flight data arrives missing or corrupted. Texas Tech's tool pulls together data from many sources. Tape drawn to illustrate.
strings: Some flight data arrives missing or corrupted. Texas Tech's tool pulls together data from many sources. Tape drawn to illustrate.

S3.headline: 37 percent of missing data restored
S3.body: In testing, Texas Tech's neural networks restored 37 percent of missing and corrupted flight data. Each gold cell is one in a hundred.
strings: In testing, Texas Tech's neural networks restored 37 percent of missing and corrupted flight data. Each gold cell is one in a hundred.

S4.headline: Data files up to 73 percent smaller
S4.body: In testing, the networks cut data volume by up to 30 percent and data files by up to 73 percent. Both figures are ceilings, not averages.
strings: Data files up to 73 percent smaller

S5.headline: 480 hour phase actions, predicted in testing
S5.body: In testing, the neural networks predicted unplanned maintenance actions. They predicted 480 hour phase maintenance actions too.
strings: 480 hour phase actions, predicted in testing

S6.headline: Texas Tech says one tool tracks engine life
S6.body: Texas Tech says the Propulsion System Validator tracks the remaining useful life of aircraft engines on its own. It recommends maintenance tied to the aviation technical manual.
strings: Texas Tech says one tool tracks engine life

S7.headline: Finding weak parts before they fail
S7.body: Texas Tech's Henry Johnston says the models help teams find weak parts and plan repairs before failure. Maintenance crews check aircraft with computers and hands on inspections.
strings: Finding weak parts before they fail

S8.headline: Lubbock to Fort Worth since 2019
S8.body: Texas Tech's institute in Lubbock and AVX Defense Technologies of Fort Worth have partnered since 2019. More than 18 students worked on the effort. Students also finished three capstone projects.
strings: Texas Tech's institute in Lubbock and AVX Defense Technologies of Fort Worth have partnered since 2019. More than 18 students worked on the effort. Students also finished three capstone projects.

S9.headline: Every result so far is from testing
S9.body: Texas Tech says both tools have been provided to the Army. Every result it reports comes from testing. The Army Aviation and Missile Command funds the program. Watch that command for the first result from service.
